stem: A 10-month-old infant has early hand preference and right-sided upper motor neuron signs (increased tone, clonus, brisk reflexes, mild weakness, and smaller right-sided limb growth), suggesting an old perinatal brain injury causing hemiplegic cerebral palsy. Which MRI finding is most likely?

options.text: A heterotopia in the left lateral ventricle
An acute ruptured arteriovenous malformation in the left middle cerebral artery
An old left middle cerebral artery territory infarct

explanation: The presentation is most consistent with spastic right hemiplegia from a prenatal or perinatal left hemispheric injury. An old left MCA territory infarct would explain the early hand preference, contralateral pyramidal signs, and reduced growth of the affected limbs. The other options do not fit this chronic unilateral upper motor neuron syndrome.
rationale: A chronic unilateral upper motor neuron pattern in an infant strongly suggests a static perinatal brain lesion, most commonly a remote arterial infarct affecting the contralateral motor cortex/internal capsule.

optionExplanations.A: Periventricular or ventricular heterotopia may cause seizures or developmental issues, but it would not typically produce this pattern of unilateral spastic hemiparesis and limb undergrowth.
optionExplanations.B: A posterior fossa mass would more likely cause ataxia, vomiting, or raised intracranial pressure, not isolated contralateral upper motor neuron signs.
optionExplanations.C: An acute ruptured AVM would present dramatically with acute neurological deficit, seizure, or haemorrhage, not a stable chronic hemiparesis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: an old left MCA infarct would cause chronic right-sided spastic hemiplegia, early hand preference, and asymmetric limb growth consistent with hemiplegic cerebral palsy.

Instructions

Question 9 - 12 relate to this case

Case 4

A mother brings her 10 month old child to see you because her son is mostly using his left hand to play with toys and she is not sure if this is just because he is going to be left handed. He is otherwise growing well and is a happy child. The child was born at 35 weeks with a birth weight of 3.1 kg. He was breastfed until a month ago and did not have problems with attachment. He rolled at 4 months and has been able to sit independently since 8 months of age. His mother states that he can commando crawl but in a ‘crab like’ fashion in that he is propelling himself with his left side. He has developed a pincer grip in the left hand but the right hand is still grasping objects.

On examination his head circumference is 43cm (3rd centile), his weight and height are on the 50th centile. His BP is 90/70. He has no neurocutaneous stigmata and he is not dysmorphic. On inspection of his limbs you notice his right big toe is smaller than his left and his thumb on the right is also smaller than the left thumb. His tone is increased on the right side and his foot can only just get into a neutral position. There is sustained clonus at the right ankle. His power is only mildly reduced on the right side compared to the left in both the upper and lower limb. His reflexes are brisk with spread on the right but normal on the left. He is able to fix and follow, his facial movements are symmetrical and his voice is strong. He turns his head when you call his name.
